tool.name: statsmodels
tool.tagline: Statistical models, tests and time series with full inference in Python
tool.description: statsmodels estimates statistical models such as linear and generalised linear regression, mixed models and ARIMA-family time series, and reports the inference around them: standard errors, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests and diagnostics. It supports R-style formulas on pandas DataFrames. Use it when you need to explain and test relationships in data, not just predict.

glossary.def: A simple rule, such as a straight line, that describes how an outcome tends to depend on some measured values, while allowing individual cases to scatter around it.
The column a model tries to explain or predict, such as price. Also called the dependent variable or, in statsmodels, endog.
A column used to explain the outcome, such as area or number of rooms. Also called an explanatory variable, regressor or, in statsmodels, exog.
In statistics, another name for the outcome a model explains (not a server's reply).
Fitting a rule that explains an outcome from one or more predictors, usually to see how the outcome changes as each predictor changes.
Regression where the rule is a straight line (or flat surface): the outcome is an intercept plus each predictor times its coefficient.
A number in a fitted model; in linear regression, how much the outcome changes per one-unit change in a predictor, holding the others fixed.
The coefficient of a predictor in a straight-line model: how much the outcome goes up (or down) for each one-unit increase of the predictor.
The model's predicted outcome when every predictor is zero; where the fitted line crosses the vertical axis.
The model's prediction for a row it was fitted on.
The real outcome minus the model's fitted value for that row: how far the row is from the fitted line.
Ordinary least squares: fitting a linear regression by choosing the coefficients that make the sum of squared residuals as small as possible.
The share of the variation in the outcome that the model accounts for, from 0 (nothing) to 1 (every row exactly on the fitted line).
The rows you actually collected, out of all the cases you'd like to draw conclusions about.
A value calculated from a sample as a best guess of an unknown true value, such as a fitted coefficient.
In statistics, how much an estimate would typically vary if you repeated the data collection; smaller means the estimate is more precise.
A range of values consistent with the data around an estimate; a 95% interval is roughly the estimate plus or minus two standard errors.
A calculation that checks whether the data are surprising under an assumed 'nothing going on' explanation (the null hypothesis).
The 'nothing going on' assumption a hypothesis test starts from, such as 'this coefficient is truly zero'.
The probability of getting a result at least as extreme as yours if the null hypothesis were true; small values (often below 0.05) count as evidence against it.
Describes a result with a p-value below an agreed cut-off (usually 0.05), so chance alone is an unlikely explanation. It says nothing about how large or important the effect is.
In statistics, drawing conclusions about the wider world from a sample, with measures of how uncertain they are (standard errors, intervals, tests).
R² with a penalty for each extra predictor, so adding useless predictors doesn't make a model look better.
A test of whether several coefficients are all zero at once, such as all predictors in a model, or the extra terms of a bigger model.
Scores for comparing models fitted to the same data: they reward a good fit and penalise extra coefficients. Lower is better; the absolute value means nothing.
A summary-table warning sign: a large value means some predictors nearly duplicate each other or have very different scales, which makes coefficients unstable.
A short text description of a model such as 'price ~ area + C(city)': the outcome left of ~, predictors on the right.
A programming language made for statistics; statsmodels' formula syntax comes from it.
The table of numbers a model is actually fitted on: one column per coefficient (including a column of ones for the intercept), built from your data and formula.
A 0/1 column standing for one category, such as 'is in Oslo'; a text column with k categories becomes k - 1 dummies.
The category left out when making dummy variables; every other category's coefficient is its difference from this one.
A model term that lets the effect of one predictor depend on the value of another, written a:b in a formula.
A range likely to contain the outcome of one new case; wider than the confidence interval for the average, because it includes individual scatter.
Predicting for predictor values outside the range of the data the model was fitted on, where the fitted pattern may not hold.
An outcome with only two possible values, such as bought or not, usually stored as 1 and 0.
A regression model for yes/no outcomes that predicts the probability of yes, using an S-shaped curve that stays between 0 and 1.
Fitting a model by choosing the coefficients under which the data you actually observed are most probable.
The probability that something happens divided by the probability that it doesn't: a 20% chance is odds of 0.25 ('1 to 4').
The natural logarithm of the odds; logistic regression coefficients are changes on this scale.
How many times the odds are multiplied per one-unit change in a predictor; exp of a logistic regression coefficient. 1 means no change.
How much a model's predicted probability (or outcome) changes per one-unit change in a predictor, often averaged over the rows of the data.
Ways of turning a category predictor into columns, which decide what each coefficient compares (for example each level against a reference level).
The plain coefficient of a predictor in a model that also has interactions with it; it is that predictor's effect where the interacting variable is at its reference level or zero.
A test of whether one or several coefficients are zero (or equal some values), based on the estimates and their standard errors.
Two models where the bigger one contains every term of the smaller one plus some more, so they can be compared with a test.
A family of regression models (including logistic and Poisson regression) that link a sum of coefficients times predictors to the outcome's average through a link function.
In a GLM, the function connecting the sum of coefficients times predictors to the outcome's average, such as the log for counts or the S-curve for probabilities.
In a GLM, the assumed kind of random variation of the outcome: Binomial for yes/no, Poisson or negative binomial for counts, Gamma for positive amounts.
How many times the event rate is multiplied per one-unit change in a predictor; exp of a Poisson model coefficient.
When counts vary much more than a Poisson model allows, which makes its standard errors too small.
How much opportunity each row had to produce events (time at risk, number of visitors); included so a count model estimates a rate.
The familiar bell-shaped pattern of values: most near the average, fewer and fewer further away on both sides.
When residuals are more spread out for some rows than others, for example growing with the fitted value; it makes the usual standard errors wrong.
A per-row measure of how much the fitted coefficients would change if that row were left out; large values flag influential points.
When predictors are strongly correlated with each other, so the model can't tell their effects apart and their standard errors grow.
Correlation of a series with its own earlier values, such as each month's residual resembling the previous month's.
An estimation method is unbiased if, averaged over many possible samples, its estimates hit the true value.
The method used to calculate standard errors (from the estimates' covariance matrix); changing it changes standard errors and p-values, never the coefficients.
Standard errors calculated in a way that stays valid when residuals are unevenly spread (heteroscedasticity).
Standard errors that allow rows in the same group (school, customer) to be related, needed when rows within groups aren't independent.
The slow, long-run upward or downward movement of a time series, ignoring repeating patterns and noise.
A pattern in a time series that repeats every fixed period, such as higher sales every December.
A step back in a time series: lag 1 is the previous value, lag 12 in monthly data is the same month last year.
The autocorrelation function: the correlation of a series with itself at each lag. The PACF shows the same after removing the effect of shorter lags.
A time series is stationary if its average level and spread don't drift over time; many forecasting models assume it.
Replacing each value of a time series by its change from an earlier value (the previous one, or the same season last year), which removes trends.
A classic forecasting model that differences a series and predicts each value from its own recent values and recent prediction errors; SARIMAX adds seasonality and outside predictors.
Predicting a series' value from its own previous values.
An outside predictor in a time series model, such as price or holidays, whose future values must be supplied to forecast.
A prediction of future values of a time series; the horizon is how far ahead it reaches.
A regression model for grouped data that adds random effects (each group's own shift) to the usual fixed coefficients.
In a mixed model, each group's own deviation (in intercept or slope), treated as drawn from a normal distribution.
In a mixed model, the ordinary coefficients that apply to everyone, interpreted like OLS coefficients.
The share of the total variation that lies between groups rather than within them; high means rows in the same group are very alike.
Pulling each group's estimate towards the overall average, more strongly for groups with little data.
Analysis of variance: a table of F-tests showing whether each term (or group difference) explains a real part of the outcome's variation.
The chance of at least one false alarm across a whole set of tests; corrections like Holm and Bonferroni keep it at the chosen level.
The expected share of false alarms among the results you declare significant; Benjamini-Hochberg controls it.
The chance that a study detects an effect of a given size if it really exists; power analysis finds the sample size needed (often for 80% power).
How big a difference or effect is, often measured in standard deviations so it can be compared across studies.
A time series model with a hidden state (such as the true level) that evolves over time, and observations that are noisy measurements of it.
The step-by-step method that estimates a state space model's hidden state after each observation and computes the likelihood; the smoother refines it using all data.
The logarithm of how probable the observed data are under a model with given coefficients; maximum likelihood makes it as large as possible.
The matrix of second derivatives of the log-likelihood, describing how sharply it curves around its peak; its inverse gives the standard errors.
An algorithm that improves a guess for the coefficients step by step until the fit stops getting better.
An optimiser converges when its steps stop changing the answer; if it doesn't, the reported estimates can't be trusted.
In a yes/no model, when a predictor splits the yeses from the noes exactly, so the best coefficient is infinitely large and the fit breaks down.
A model is identified when only one set of coefficients fits best; with duplicated predictors many sets fit equally well, and individual coefficients are meaningless.

concepts.name: Regression in plain words
concepts.summary: What a statistical model is: a line fitted through data that says how an outcome changes with the things you measured.
concepts.why: Every statsmodels result is about a fitted model, so you need its basic parts before reading any output.
concepts.body:
Suppose you have a table of flats: each row has the floor area and the price it sold for. Bigger flats tend to cost more, but not exactly in step; two flats of the same size can sell for different prices. A **statistical model** is a simple rule that captures the general pattern while admitting that individual rows scatter around it.

The most common model is a straight line: `price = a + b * area`. The column you want to explain (price) is the **outcome**. The columns you use to explain it (area) are the **predictors**. Finding the line that fits a table of data best is called **regression**; with a straight-line rule it's called **linear regression**.

The numbers in the rule are its **coefficients**. `b`, the **slope**, says how much the outcome changes when the predictor goes up by one: "each extra square metre adds about 2.4 to the price". `a`, the **intercept**, is the predicted outcome when every predictor is zero, the height where the line crosses the vertical axis.

For each row, the model's prediction is called the **fitted value**. The gap between the real outcome and the fitted value is the **residual**: positive when the flat sold for more than the line predicts, negative when it sold for less.

How do we pick the "best" line? The usual method squares every residual (so big misses count a lot and signs don't cancel) and chooses the coefficients that make the sum of those squares as small as possible. This is **ordinary least squares**, or **OLS**.

A model can have several predictors: `price = a + b1 * area + b2 * rooms`. Then each coefficient is the effect of its own predictor **while the others stay the same**: b2 compares flats of equal area that differ by one room.

Finally, **R²** ("R squared") summarises how well the line fits: the share of the ups and downs in the outcome that the predictors account for, from 0 (nothing) to 1 (every row exactly on the line).
concepts.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

flats = pd.DataFrame({"area":  [40, 55, 60, 75, 90, 110],
                      "price": [130, 165, 175, 215, 240, 300]})

model = smf.ols("price ~ area", data=flats).fit()   # fit price = a + b * area
print(model.params.round(2).to_dict())   # {'Intercept': 33.31, 'area': 2.38}

fitted = model.fittedvalues              # the line's prediction for each row
print(fitted.round(1).tolist()[:2])      # [128.7, 164.4]
print(model.resid.round(1).tolist()[:2]) # [1.3, 0.6]  (real price minus prediction)
print(round(model.rsquared, 3))          # 0.995  (the line explains almost everything)
takeaways: A model explains an outcome from predictors; regression finds the best-fitting rule
Coefficients: the slope is the change in outcome per unit of a predictor; the intercept is the value at zero
Residual = real outcome minus fitted value; OLS makes the sum of squared residuals as small as possible
R² is the share of variation the model explains (0 to 1)
pitfalls: Reading a coefficient as what happens when you change only that predictor in the real world; it describes the pattern in the data, which isn't necessarily cause and effect.

quiz.q: A model says price = 30 + 2.5 * area. A 100 m² flat sold for 300. What is its residual?
quiz.explain: The fitted value is 30 + 2.5 * 100 = 280, and the residual is 300 - 280 = 20.

quiz.q: In price = a + b1 * area + b2 * rooms, what does b2 describe?
options: The price of a flat with no rooms
The price change for one more room, comparing flats of the same area
quiz.explain: With several predictors, each coefficient is the effect of its predictor while the others are held fixed.

concepts.name: Uncertainty: standard errors and p-values
concepts.summary: Why every estimate comes with uncertainty, and what standard errors, confidence intervals and p-values tell you about it.
concepts.why: statsmodels' main strength is reporting how sure you can be about each coefficient, and these three numbers are how it does that.
concepts.body:
Your table is a **sample**: a few hundred flats out of all the flats that exist. Collect a different sample and the fitted slope would come out a little different. So a coefficient is an **estimate**, a best guess from the data you happen to have, and the question is how far off it might be.

The **standard error** answers that. It's the typical amount an estimate would move around if you repeated the whole data collection many times. A slope of 2.5 with a standard error of 0.05 is pinned down tightly; with a standard error of 2 it is very vague. More rows and less scatter give smaller standard errors.

A **confidence interval** turns that into a range. The usual 95% interval is roughly the estimate plus or minus two standard errors, say [2.4, 2.6]. Loosely: the values inside are the ones consistent with your data. If you repeated the study many times, about 95% of the intervals computed this way would contain the true value.

Often you want to know whether a predictor matters at all. A **hypothesis test** starts by assuming the boring answer, the **null hypothesis**: "the true coefficient is zero; this predictor has no effect". It then asks how surprising your estimate would be if that were true.

The answer is the **p-value**: the probability of getting an estimate at least this far from zero purely by chance, if the true value were zero. A small p-value (below 0.05 is the common convention) means chance alone is an unlikely explanation, and the result is called **statistically significant**.

Two warnings. A small p-value does not mean the effect is large or important; with lots of data, tiny effects become significant. And a large p-value does not prove there is no effect; it may only mean your data are too few or too noisy to tell.

All of these numbers are only trustworthy if the model's assumptions roughly hold, which later lessons show how to check. Using a sample to draw conclusions like this is called statistical **inference**.
concepts.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
df = pd.DataFrame({"area": rng.uniform(40, 150, 100), "luck": rng.normal(size=100)})
df["price"] = 20 + 2.5 * df["area"] + rng.normal(0, 15, 100)   # luck plays no part

res = smf.ols("price ~ area + luck", data=df).fit()
print(res.params.round(2).to_dict())   # estimates
print(res.bse.round(2).to_dict())      # standard errors: how far off they might be
print(res.conf_int().loc["area"].round(2).tolist())   # 95% interval around 2.5
print(res.pvalues.round(3).to_dict())  # area tiny (real effect), luck large (no evidence)
takeaways: A coefficient is an estimate from a sample; its standard error says how much it could vary
A 95% confidence interval is roughly the estimate plus or minus two standard errors
The p-value asks how surprising the estimate would be if the true effect were zero
Significant does not mean large, and not significant does not mean zero
pitfalls: Treating p = 0.06 as "no effect" and p = 0.04 as "proven"; they are nearly the same amount of evidence.

quiz.q: A coefficient is 3.0 with a standard error of 0.5. Which 95% confidence interval is about right?
quiz.explain: Roughly two standard errors either side: 3.0 plus or minus 1.0.

quiz.q: A predictor's p-value is 0.40. What can you conclude?
options: The predictor definitely has no effect
The effect is 40% likely to be real
The data give no clear evidence that the effect differs from zero
quiz.explain: A large p-value means chance could easily explain the estimate; it is absence of evidence, not proof of no effect.

concepts.name: Linear regression with OLS
concepts.summary: Fit an ordinary least squares model with statsmodels.api and read its coefficients, standard errors and fit from the results object.
concepts.why: statsmodels gives you not just predictions but standard errors, p-values and confidence intervals for every coefficient.
concepts.body:
statsmodels offers two ways to describe a model. `statsmodels.api` (imported as `sm`) takes the outcome and the predictor columns directly as DataFrames or arrays; `statsmodels.formula.api` (`smf`) takes a short text formula, covered in the next lesson. This lesson uses `sm`.

Fitting is two steps: build a **model** from data, then call `.fit()` to estimate the coefficients and get a **results** object:

```python
X = sm.add_constant(df[["area", "rooms"]])
res = sm.OLS(df["price"], X).fit()
```

Note the argument order: **outcome first, then predictors**. (If you know the machine-learning library scikit-learn, it's the other way round there.) By convention the outcome is called `y` and the table of predictors `X`.

`sm.OLS` also does **not** add an intercept for you. `sm.add_constant` adds a column of ones named `const`, and its coefficient becomes the intercept. Without it the line is forced through zero, which is rarely what you want.

The results object holds everything:

- `res.params`: the coefficients, labelled with the column names,
- `res.bse`: their standard errors, plus `res.pvalues` and `res.conf_int()`,
- `res.rsquared` for R², and more fit measures you'll meet in the summary lesson,
- `res.resid` and `res.fittedvalues`: residuals and fitted values per row,
- `res.summary()`: everything as one printed table.

Passing pandas objects is worth it: coefficients, residuals and predictions keep the column names and the index. Rows with missing values make fitting fail by default; pass `missing="drop"` or clean the data first.
concepts.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.api as sm

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
df = pd.DataFrame({"area": rng.uniform(40, 150, 100), "rooms": rng.integers(1, 6, 100)})
df["price"] = 20 + 2.5 * df["area"] + 10 * df["rooms"] + rng.normal(0, 15, 100)

X = sm.add_constant(df[["area", "rooms"]])   # adds a 'const' column of ones
res = sm.OLS(df["price"], X).fit()           # y first, then X

print(res.params.round(2).to_dict())   # {'const': 20.06, 'area': 2.51, 'rooms': 9.08}
print(res.bse.round(2).to_dict())      # {'const': 6.05, 'area': 0.05, 'rooms': 1.1}
print(round(res.rsquared, 3))          # 0.967
print(res.conf_int().loc["area"].round(2).tolist())  # [2.41, 2.61]
takeaways: `sm.OLS(y, X).fit()`: outcome first, then predictors
Add the intercept yourself with `sm.add_constant`
The results object holds coefficients, standard errors, p-values and fit measures
pitfalls: Forgetting `add_constant`, which forces the regression line through zero.

quiz.q: You fit sm.OLS(y, df[["x"]]).fit() and get one coefficient and no intercept. Why?
options: statsmodels drops intercepts when there is one predictor
The intercept is stored in res.bse
y and X are in the wrong order
sm.OLS does not add a constant column automatically
quiz.explain: With sm you add the intercept column (a column of ones) yourself with sm.add_constant.

concepts.name: Model formulas
concepts.summary: Describe models as short formulas like 'price ~ area + C(city)' and let statsmodels build the predictor columns for you.
concepts.why: Formulas handle intercepts, text categories and calculated columns in one readable string.
concepts.body:
`statsmodels.formula.api` (imported as `smf`) fits a model from a **formula** and a DataFrame: `smf.ols("price ~ area + rooms", data=df).fit()`. The formula is a small text language borrowed from the statistics language R. Left of `~` is the outcome; right of it, the predictors joined by `+`.

From the formula, statsmodels builds the actual table of numbers the model uses, called the **design matrix**: one column per coefficient. Doing that by hand is fiddly, which is the point of formulas:

- an **intercept is included automatically**; remove it with `- 1` or `+ 0`,
- text columns, such as a city name, are turned into numbers automatically (next paragraph); `C(zip_code)` forces that treatment for number codes that are really labels,
- functions work inline: `np.log(income)`, or `standardize(x)` to rescale x to mean 0 and spread 1,
- ordinary arithmetic needs `I(...)`, because `+` and `*` have formula meanings: `I(area ** 2)`, `I(price / 1000)`.

A model can only multiply numbers, so a text column like `city` with values Lima, Oslo and Rome becomes **dummy variables**: one 0/1 column per city except one. A row gets 1 in the `Oslo` column if it's in Oslo, else 0. The city left out (here Lima, first alphabetically) is the **reference level**, and each city's coefficient is its difference from Lima.

`a * b` is shorthand for `a + b + a:b`, where `a:b` is an **interaction**: it lets the effect of `a` depend on the value of `b` (a later lesson covers it).

Most models have formula versions with lowercase names: `smf.ols`, `smf.logit`, `smf.glm`, `smf.mixedlm`. Rows with missing values in the columns used are dropped silently; compare `res.nobs` (rows used) with `len(df)` to notice. The formula is stored with the results, so `res.predict(new_df)` applies the same steps, including the same dummy columns, to new data.
concepts.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
df = pd.DataFrame({"area": rng.uniform(40, 150, 120),
                   "city": rng.choice(["Oslo", "Rome", "Lima"], 120)})
bonus = df["city"].map({"Lima": 0, "Oslo": 60, "Rome": 30})
df["price"] = 50 + 2 * df["area"] + bonus + rng.normal(0, 10, 120)

res = smf.ols("price ~ area + C(city)", data=df).fit()
print(res.params.round(1).to_dict())
# {'Intercept': 43.4, 'C(city)[T.Oslo]': 61.6, 'C(city)[T.Rome]': 31.4, 'area': 2.0}

res2 = smf.ols("np.log(price) ~ area + I(area ** 2)", data=df).fit()
print(list(res2.params.index))   # ['Intercept', 'area', 'I(area ** 2)']

new = pd.DataFrame({"area": [100], "city": ["Rome"]})
print(res.predict(new).round(1).tolist())   # [279.0]
takeaways: `smf.ols("y ~ a + b", data=df)` adds the intercept and turns text columns into dummy variables
Use `C()` for number codes that are labels and `I()` for arithmetic
`predict(new_df)` re-applies the formula's steps to new data
pitfalls: Writing `y ~ x**2` instead of `y ~ I(x**2)`, which does not square x.

quiz.q: What does the formula `y ~ a * b` fit?
options: a, b and their interaction a:b
Only the product a times b
a and b without an intercept
The ratio of a and b
quiz.explain: In formulas, * expands to a + b + a:b; use I(a * b) for the arithmetic product.

concepts.name: Reading a regression summary
concepts.summary: Read the three blocks of res.summary(): fit measures, the coefficient table, and the checks on residuals.
concepts.why: The summary table is what you report and decide from, so you must read it correctly.
concepts.body:
`res.summary()` prints three blocks. Most of it uses ideas you've met; this lesson names the rest.

**Top block (overall fit)**: the number of rows used (`No. Observations`) and **R²**. Next to it is **adjusted R²**: R² always creeps up when you add any predictor, even a useless one, so the adjusted version subtracts a penalty per predictor and is fairer for comparing models.

The **F-statistic** and `Prob (F-statistic)` are a test of all predictors at once: its null hypothesis is "none of the predictors matter". A tiny value means the model explains something.

`Log-Likelihood`, **AIC** and **BIC** are scores for comparing different models fitted to the same rows. Each rewards fitting the data well and penalises extra coefficients; lower AIC or BIC is better. Their absolute values mean nothing on their own.

**Coefficient table**, one row per coefficient:

- `coef`: the estimate, the change in the outcome for a one-unit change in that predictor, holding the others fixed,
- `std err`: its standard error,
- `t` = coef / std err, how many standard errors the estimate is from zero, and `P>|t|`, the p-value for "this coefficient is zero",
- `[0.025 0.975]`: the lower and upper ends of the 95% confidence interval.

**Bottom block (residual checks)**: tests of whether the residuals behave as the method assumes, covered in the diagnostics lesson. `Omnibus` and `Jarque-Bera` check that residuals follow the familiar bell-shaped curve; `Durbin-Watson` near 2 means neighbouring rows' residuals aren't linked. A large **condition number** comes with a printed note when predictors nearly duplicate each other or have wildly different scales, which makes coefficients unstable.

In code, use `res.params`, `res.pvalues`, `res.conf_int()`, or `res.summary2().tables[1]` for the coefficient table as a DataFrame.
concepts.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
df = pd.DataFrame({"ads": rng.uniform(0, 10, 80), "noise": rng.normal(size=80)})
df["sales"] = 5 + 1.5 * df["ads"] + rng.normal(0, 3, 80)

res = smf.ols("sales ~ ads + noise", data=df).fit()
table = res.summary2().tables[1]               # coefficient table as a DataFrame
print(table[["Coef.", "Std.Err.", "P>|t|"]].round(3))
#            Coef.  Std.Err.  P>|t|
# Intercept  4.250     0.813  0.000
# ads        1.644     0.140  0.000
# noise     -0.067     0.423  0.874   (no evidence of an effect)
print(round(res.rsquared, 3), round(res.rsquared_adj, 3))   # 0.642 0.632
print(f"{res.f_pvalue:.1e}")                              # 7.0e-18
takeaways: coef = effect of a one-unit change holding the other predictors fixed
The p-value tests coef = 0; the confidence interval shows the plausible range
Use AIC/BIC and adjusted R² to compare models fitted to the same data
pitfalls: Reading a large p-value as proof that a predictor has no effect.

quiz.q: In a summary, a coefficient is 0.8 with 95% CI [0.1, 1.5]. Which statement is right?
options: The data are consistent with effects from about 0.1 to 1.5
The predictor causes y to increase
quiz.explain: The interval excludes 0 (so p < 0.05) and shows the range of effects compatible with the data; it says nothing about cause.

concepts.name: Prediction and confidence intervals
concepts.summary: Predict new values and quantify their uncertainty with get_prediction and summary_frame.
concepts.why: A point prediction without an interval hides how wrong it could be.
concepts.body:
`res.predict(new_data)` returns predictions: one number per new row. To see how uncertain each one is, use `res.get_prediction(new_data).summary_frame(alpha=0.05)`, which returns a DataFrame with:

- `mean`: the predicted value,
- `mean_ci_lower`, `mean_ci_upper`: the **confidence interval** for the *average* outcome of all rows with those predictor values,
- `obs_ci_lower`, `obs_ci_upper`: the **prediction interval** for *one* new row.

The difference matters. The confidence interval only reflects how unsure we are about the fitted line itself, and it shrinks as you collect more data. The prediction interval adds the scatter of individual rows around the line, which more data can't remove. So it is always wider. "What is the average price of 100 m² flats?" needs the first; "what will this particular flat sell for?" needs the second.

With a formula model, pass a DataFrame with the original column names and the formula is applied automatically. With `sm`, `new_data` must have the same columns, including the constant. Use `sm.add_constant(new_X, has_constant="add")`: with a single new row, every column looks constant, and `add_constant` would otherwise skip adding one.

`alpha=0.05` means 95% intervals; `alpha=0.1` gives 90%.

The intervals assume the model is right and that residuals are spread evenly along the line in a bell-shaped pattern. Predicting far outside the range of the data you fitted on is called **extrapolation**, and there the intervals are too optimistic: the straight line may simply not hold.
concepts.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
df = pd.DataFrame({"area": rng.uniform(40, 150, 200)})
df["price"] = 30 + 2.5 * df["area"] + rng.normal(0, 20, 200)
res = smf.ols("price ~ area", data=df).fit()

new = pd.DataFrame({"area": [60, 100, 140]})
frame = res.get_prediction(new).summary_frame(alpha=0.05)
print(frame[["mean", "mean_ci_lower", "mean_ci_upper", "obs_ci_lower", "obs_ci_upper"]].round(1))
#     mean  mean_ci_lower  mean_ci_upper  obs_ci_lower  obs_ci_upper
# 0  181.5          177.2          185.9         142.4         220.6
# 1  280.5          277.7          283.2         241.5         319.4
# 2  379.4          374.5          384.3         340.2         418.6
takeaways: `get_prediction(...).summary_frame()` gives predictions and both interval types
Confidence intervals cover the average outcome; prediction intervals cover one new row
Prediction intervals are always wider
pitfalls: Quoting the confidence interval as the range for an individual future value.

quiz.q: Which interval should you give for the sale price of one specific new house?
options: The confidence interval of the mean (mean_ci)
quiz.explain: A single observation includes residual noise, which only the prediction interval accounts for.

concepts.name: Logistic regression and odds ratios
concepts.summary: Model a yes/no outcome with logistic regression (Logit), and turn its coefficients into odds ratios and changes in probability.
concepts.why: Yes/no outcomes (bought, cancelled, defaulted) are everywhere, and their coefficients need special interpretation.
concepts.body:
Some outcomes are yes or no: did the visitor buy? Stored as 1 and 0, that's a **binary outcome**. A straight line is a bad fit: it would predict values above 1 or below 0. **Logistic regression** instead models the probability of a 1, bending the line into an S-shaped curve that always stays between 0 and 1.

```python
res = smf.logit("bought ~ discount + visits", data=df).fit()
```

It isn't fitted by least squares but by **maximum likelihood**: the coefficients chosen are the ones under which the outcomes you actually saw are most probable. The results object looks the same, with standard errors and p-values. (scikit-learn's `LogisticRegression`, by contrast, shrinks coefficients towards zero by default, so its numbers differ.)

Interpreting coefficients takes one new idea: **odds**, the probability of yes divided by the probability of no. A 20% chance is odds of 0.2 / 0.8 = 0.25, "1 to 4". Logit coefficients are changes in the logarithm of the odds (**log-odds**), which is hard to picture. So exponentiate them: `np.exp(res.params)` gives **odds ratios**. An odds ratio of 1.5 means each extra unit multiplies the odds by 1.5 (50% higher); below 1 means lower. Exponentiate the interval ends too: `np.exp(res.conf_int())`.

Odds ratios are not probability ratios: an odds ratio of 2 doesn't mean "twice as likely". For effects in plain probability, `res.get_margeff().summary_frame()` reports the **average marginal effect**: how much the predicted probability changes per unit of each predictor, averaged over your rows.

`res.predict(new)` returns probabilities. `res.prsquared` is a rough R²-like fit measure for logit. The fitter prints progress messages; pass `disp=0` to silence them. If one predictor splits the yeses from the noes perfectly, the method breaks down: you get huge coefficients or a `PerfectSeparationWarning` (an Expert lesson covers this).
concepts.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
n = 2000
df = pd.DataFrame({"discount": rng.integers(0, 2, n), "visits": rng.poisson(3, n)})
logit_p = -2 + 0.7 * df["discount"] + 0.3 * df["visits"]
df["bought"] = rng.binomial(1, 1 / (1 + np.exp(-logit_p)))

res = smf.logit("bought ~ discount + visits", data=df).fit(disp=0)
print(res.params.round(2).to_dict())     # {'Intercept': -1.97, 'discount': 0.84, 'visits': 0.29}
print(np.exp(res.params).round(2).to_dict())
# {'Intercept': 0.14, 'discount': 2.32, 'visits': 1.33}  (odds ratios)

me = res.get_margeff().summary_frame()
print(me["dy/dx"].round(3).to_dict())    # {'discount': 0.175, 'visits': 0.06}
print(res.predict(pd.DataFrame({"discount": [1], "visits": [5]})).round(3).tolist())  # [0.578]
takeaways: Logit models the probability of a yes; coefficients are changes in log-odds
`np.exp(res.params)` gives odds ratios; `get_margeff()` gives effects on probability
statsmodels' Logit doesn't shrink coefficients, unlike scikit-learn's default
pitfalls: Describing an odds ratio of 2 as 'twice as likely'.

quiz.q: A logit coefficient for 'discount' is 0.69. What is the odds ratio?
quiz.explain: exp(0.69) is about 2, so a discount roughly doubles the odds of buying.

concepts.name: Categories, contrasts and interactions
concepts.summary: Choose reference levels, read dummy coefficients and model effects that depend on each other.
concepts.why: Most real questions are about groups and about whether an effect differs between groups.
concepts.body:
A category predictor with k values (levels) becomes k - 1 dummy columns. The level left out is the reference, and each coefficient is the difference from it. By default the reference is the first level alphabetically, which may not be meaningful. Choose it with **treatment coding**: `C(city, Treatment(reference="Rome"))`. Other ways of coding categories (**contrasts**) exist, such as `Sum`, where each coefficient is a level's difference from the average of all levels.

An **interaction** lets the effect of one variable depend on another. `price ~ area * C(city)` fits a separate area slope per city: the `area` coefficient is the slope in the reference city, and `area:C(city)[T.Oslo]` is how much steeper or flatter it is in Oslo. With interactions, the plain `area` coefficient (the **main effect**) is no longer "the effect of area"; it is the effect at the reference level (or, for a number predictor in the interaction, where that number is zero, which is why subtracting its mean first, **centring**, helps).

To test whether a whole category predictor or interaction matters, test all its coefficients together (a joint test) rather than reading individual p-values:

- `res.wald_test_terms()` runs a **Wald test** per term: are all its coefficients zero together?
- `sm.stats.anova_lm(res_small, res_big)` compares a model with a bigger one that contains all its terms plus more (**nested models**), using an F-test,
- `res.f_test("area:C(city)[T.Oslo] = 0")` tests any equation about the coefficients you write.

Too many interactions quickly overfit (fit the noise of this sample rather than a real pattern); add them because you have a reason to expect the effect to differ.
concepts.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.api as sm
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
df = pd.DataFrame({"area": rng.uniform(40, 150, 300),
                   "city": rng.choice(["Oslo", "Rome", "Lima"], 300)})
slope = df["city"].map({"Lima": 1.0, "Oslo": 3.0, "Rome": 2.0})
df["price"] = 40 + slope * df["area"] + rng.normal(0, 15, 300)

f = "price ~ area * C(city, Treatment(reference='Rome'))"
res = smf.ols(f, data=df).fit()
print(res.params.filter(like="area").round(2).tolist())   # [2.04, -1.08, 1.0]
# Rome slope 2.0; Lima is 1.0 lower; Oslo is 1.0 higher

small = smf.ols("price ~ area + C(city)", data=df).fit()
print(sm.stats.anova_lm(small, res).round(3)[["F", "Pr(>F)"]].iloc[1].tolist())
# [448.065, 0.0]  (interaction clearly needed)
takeaways: Each dummy coefficient is a difference from the reference level
Set the reference with `C(x, Treatment(reference=...))`
Test whole category predictors and interactions jointly with F or Wald tests
pitfalls: Interpreting a main effect as the overall effect when an interaction with it is in the model.

quiz.q: In `y ~ x * C(group)` with reference 'A', what does the `x` coefficient represent?
options: The slope of x in group A
The average slope of x across all groups
The difference in slopes between groups
quiz.explain: With an interaction, the main effect of x is its slope at the reference level of group.

concepts.name: Generalised linear models
concepts.summary: Model counts, rates, proportions and skewed positive outcomes with GLM families and link functions.
concepts.why: Many outcomes are not normal; GLMs model them correctly instead of forcing them into OLS.
concepts.body:
Logistic regression is one member of a bigger group. A **generalised linear model** (GLM) has three parts: the usual sum of coefficients times predictors (`b0 + b1*x1 + ...`), a **link function** that converts that sum into the average outcome (for logit, the S-curve), and a **family**: the kind of random variation the outcome has around that average (yes/no, counts, positive amounts...). In statsmodels: `smf.glm("y ~ x", data=df, family=sm.families.Poisson()).fit()`.

Common choices:

- `Binomial()` (logit link): binary outcomes or proportions,
- `Poisson()` (log link): counts such as claims or visits; exponentiated coefficients are **rate ratios** (1.2 = 20% more events per unit),
- `NegativeBinomial(alpha=...)` (or `smf.negativebinomial`): counts that vary more than a Poisson model allows, i.e. variance well above the mean (**overdispersion**),
- `Gamma(link=sm.families.links.Log())`: positive amounts with a long tail of large values, such as claim sizes,
- `Tweedie(var_power=1.5)`: amounts that are often exactly zero and otherwise positive, such as yearly insurance losses.

For rates, include **exposure**, how long or how much each row had the chance to produce events: claims per policy-year or clicks per impression. Pass `exposure=df["years"]` (or the equivalent `offset=np.log(df["years"])`) so the model estimates a rate, not a raw count.

Check overdispersion for Poisson models: `res.pearson_chi2 / res.df_resid` well above 1 means standard errors are too small. Switch to negative binomial, or use `scale="X2"` in `fit` to rescale them.

GLM results include `deviance` (a misfit score, lower is better), `aic` and `pearson_chi2`, and `predict` returns values in the outcome's own units (counts, probabilities) by default.
concepts.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.api as sm
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

rng = np.random.default_rng(6)
n = 1000
df = pd.DataFrame({"young": rng.integers(0, 2, n), "years": rng.uniform(0.5, 3, n)})
rate = np.exp(-2.0 + 0.6 * df["young"])            # claims per policy-year
df["claims"] = rng.poisson(rate * df["years"])

res = smf.glm("claims ~ young", data=df, family=sm.families.Poisson(),
              exposure=df["years"]).fit()
print(res.params.round(2).to_dict())         # {'Intercept': -1.99, 'young': 0.58}
print(np.exp(res.params["young"]).round(2))  # 1.78 (young drivers: 78% higher claim rate)
print(round(res.pearson_chi2 / res.df_resid, 2))   # 0.89 (no overdispersion)
takeaways: Pick the family from the outcome type and the link from how effects combine
Use `exposure=` or `offset=` to model rates
Check Poisson overdispersion via Pearson chi² / df
pitfalls: Modelling counts per varying exposure without an offset, which confuses rate with exposure.

quiz.q: You model claim counts where policies were active for different lengths of time. What should you add?
quiz.explain: The exposure turns the model into one for claims per unit time, the quantity of interest.

concepts.name: Regression diagnostics
concepts.summary: Check residuals, heteroscedasticity, influential points and multicollinearity before trusting a model.
concepts.why: Standard errors, p-values and intervals are only as good as the model's assumptions, and diagnostics tell you when those fail.
concepts.body:
Every p-value and interval from OLS rests on assumptions: the right shape of relationship (a line, not a curve, unless you added terms for it), residuals that are independent of each other, residuals equally spread everywhere, residuals roughly following the bell-shaped **normal distribution**, and no single row dominating. statsmodels has a test or plot for each.

**Functional form and variance**: plot `res.resid` against `res.fittedvalues`. A curve suggests a missing term such as `I(x ** 2)`; a funnel shape, residuals spreading wider as fitted values grow, is **heteroscedasticity** (unequal spread). Test it with `het_breuschpagan(res.resid, res.model.exog)` from `statsmodels.stats.diagnostic`. `linear_reset(res)` tests for omitted non-linearity.

**Normality**: `sm.qqplot(res.resid, line="s")` plots residuals against what a normal distribution would give, so points on the line mean normal residuals; the summary's Jarque-Bera test checks the same. With large samples, mild non-normality barely matters for coefficient inference.

**Influence** (how much one row moves the fit): `infl = res.get_influence()` gives leverage (`hat_matrix_diag`, how unusual a row's predictor values are), studentized residuals (residuals rescaled so they're comparable) and **Cook's distance** (`infl.cooks_distance[0]`, how much the coefficients change if that row is removed). A common rule of thumb flags points with Cook's distance above 4/n. `sm.graphics.influence_plot(res)` shows them. Investigate flagged points; don't delete them automatically.

**Multicollinearity** (predictors that nearly duplicate each other): `variance_inflation_factor(exog, i)` from `statsmodels.stats.outliers_influence`, where `exog` is the design matrix; values above roughly 5-10 mean that predictor's standard error is inflated by its correlation with other predictors. The summary's condition number warns about the same thing.

**Autocorrelation** (in time-ordered data, each residual resembling the one before): the Durbin-Watson statistic and `acorr_ljungbox(res.resid)`.
concepts.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
from statsmodels.stats.diagnostic import het_breuschpagan
from statsmodels.stats.outliers_influence import variance_inflation_factor

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
df = pd.DataFrame({"x1": rng.uniform(1, 10, 200)})
df["x2"] = df["x1"] * 0.9 + rng.normal(0, 0.5, 200)        # nearly collinear with x1
df["y"] = 3 + 2 * df["x1"] + rng.normal(0, df["x1"])        # noise grows with x1
res = smf.ols("y ~ x1 + x2", data=df).fit()

lm_stat, lm_p, f_stat, f_p = het_breuschpagan(res.resid, res.model.exog)
print(f"{lm_p:.1e}")             # 3.8e-07 (heteroscedasticity detected)

exog = res.model.exog
print([round(float(variance_inflation_factor(exog, i)), 1) for i in (1, 2)])   # [24.9, 24.9]

cooks = res.get_influence().cooks_distance[0]
print((cooks > 4 / len(df)).sum())   # 12 (points worth a look)
takeaways: Plot residuals vs fitted values first
Test heteroscedasticity with Breusch-Pagan; check VIF for collinearity
Use Cook's distance to find influential observations
pitfalls: Deleting every flagged influential point instead of understanding why it is unusual.

quiz.q: Residuals fan out as fitted values grow. Which problem is this and what does it affect most?
options: Heteroscedasticity; the standard errors and p-values
quiz.explain: Non-constant variance leaves OLS coefficients unbiased but makes the usual standard errors wrong.

concepts.name: Robust and clustered standard errors
concepts.summary: Get valid standard errors under heteroscedasticity or clustered data with cov_type options.
concepts.why: Wrong standard errors produce falsely confident conclusions even when the coefficients are fine.
concepts.body:
When residuals are unevenly spread, or rows come in groups that share something (students in schools, several purchases by the same customer), OLS coefficients are still right on average (**unbiased**), but the default standard errors are wrong, usually too small.

The fix is to keep the estimates and change how the standard errors are calculated (the **covariance estimator**) at fit time with `cov_type`:

- `fit(cov_type="HC3")`: heteroscedasticity-consistent ("robust", "White") standard errors. HC3 behaves best in small samples; HC0-HC2 also exist.
- `fit(cov_type="cluster", cov_kwds={"groups": df["school_id"]})`: **clustered standard errors**, which allow rows in the same group to be related in any way. You need a reasonable number of groups (dozens, not five).
- `fit(cov_type="HAC", cov_kwds={"maxlags": 4})`: Newey-West standard errors for data ordered in time, where residuals are autocorrelated.

Coefficients are identical across these options; only `bse`, `pvalues`, `conf_int()` and the tests change. The summary notes which covariance type was used.

`cov_type` also works for GLM and discrete models such as `logit`. When you also want to model how rows within a group are related, mixed models (an Advanced lesson) or GEE (generalised estimating equations) are the next step.

In practice, robust standard errors are a cheap default for data measured once per unit, and clustering by the group where treatment was assigned or sampling happened is essential in experiments and in data that follows the same units over time.
concepts.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

rng = np.random.default_rng(8)
schools = np.repeat(np.arange(40), 25)                   # 40 schools x 25 students
tutoring = rng.integers(0, 2, 40)[schools]               # assigned per school
school_effect = rng.normal(0, 5, 40)[schools]
df = pd.DataFrame({"school": schools, "tutoring": tutoring,
                   "score": 60 + 3 * tutoring + school_effect + rng.normal(0, 5, 1000)})

naive = smf.ols("score ~ tutoring", data=df).fit()
robust = smf.ols("score ~ tutoring", data=df).fit(cov_type="HC3")
clustered = smf.ols("score ~ tutoring", data=df).fit(
    cov_type="cluster", cov_kwds={"groups": df["school"]})

for r in (naive, robust, clustered):
    print(round(r.params["tutoring"], 2), round(r.bse["tutoring"], 2), round(r.pvalues["tutoring"], 4))
# 2.8 0.49 0.0      (same coefficient everywhere...)
# 2.8 0.49 0.0
# 2.8 1.91 0.1424   (...but the honest uncertainty is 4x larger)
takeaways: `cov_type` changes standard errors, never coefficients
HC3 for heteroscedasticity, cluster for grouped data, HAC for autocorrelation
Cluster at the level where treatment or sampling happened
pitfalls: Using default standard errors when the treatment was assigned to groups, not individuals.

quiz.q: Treatment was assigned per school but you analyse students. Which standard errors are appropriate?
quiz.explain: Students in a school share shocks, so errors must be allowed to correlate within schools.

concepts.name: Decomposition, ACF and stationarity
concepts.summary: Decompose series into trend and seasonality, read ACF/PACF plots and test for stationarity.
concepts.why: Every forecasting model choice starts from understanding trend, seasonality and autocorrelation.
concepts.body:
statsmodels' time series tools live in `statsmodels.tsa`. Give them a pandas Series with a `DatetimeIndex` and a frequency (`series.asfreq("MS")`) so dates carry through to results and forecasts.

**Decomposition** splits a series into a **trend** (the slow long-run movement), a **seasonal** part (a pattern repeating every period, such as every 12 months) and what's left over. `STL(series, period=12).fit()` (from `statsmodels.tsa.seasonal`) copes well with outliers and changing patterns; the older `seasonal_decompose` uses moving averages (each point replaced by the average of its neighbours). Plot the result with `.plot()`.

**Autocorrelation**: `acf(x, nlags)` and `pacf(x, nlags)` (in `statsmodels.tsa.stattools`), or `plot_acf` / `plot_pacf` from `statsmodels.graphics.tsaplots`. A **lag** is a step back in time: lag 1 is the previous value. The **ACF** (autocorrelation function) shows how strongly the series correlates with itself at each lag; the **PACF** (partial ACF) shows the correlation at a lag after removing what shorter lags already explain. Slowly decaying ACF suggests a trend; spikes at lag 12 in monthly data suggest yearly seasonality.

**Stationarity**: many models assume the series' average level and spread don't drift over time; such a series is **stationary**. The **ADF test** `adfuller(x, result_object=True)` (read `.pvalue`) has the null hypothesis "the series is not stationary" (technically, it has a unit root); a small p-value suggests stationarity. **KPSS** `kpss(x)` has the opposite null, so using both is informative.

**Differencing**, replacing each value by its change from the previous one (`x.diff()`), or from the same month last year (`x.diff(12)`), usually makes a series stationary. Taking the logarithm (`np.log(x)`) first tames a spread that grows with the level.

Never shuffle time series to test a model: hold out the last part of the series and check predictions on it.
concepts.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from statsmodels.tsa.seasonal import STL
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import acf, adfuller

rng = np.random.default_rng(9)
idx = pd.date_range("2015-01-01", periods=96, freq="MS")
t = np.arange(96)
y = pd.Series(100 + 0.8 * t + 10 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * t / 12) + rng.normal(0, 2, 96), index=idx)

stl = STL(y, period=12).fit()
print(stl.seasonal.iloc[:3].round(1).tolist())    # [-0.5, 7.6, 7.8] (seasonal pattern)

print(round(adfuller(y, result_object=True).pvalue, 3))   # 0.99 (trend: not stationary)
print(round(adfuller(y.diff(12).dropna(), result_object=True).pvalue, 3))  # 0.0

print(acf(y.diff().dropna(), nlags=12)[[1, 6, 12]].round(2))   # [ 0.3 -0.6  0.6]
takeaways: Use a Series with a DatetimeIndex and frequency
STL separates trend, seasonality and remainder
ADF null = non-stationary; difference to remove trend and seasonality
pitfalls: Reading a high ADF p-value as proof of stationarity; the null is non-stationarity.

quiz.q: adfuller returns a p-value of 0.70 for your series. What does it suggest?
options: You cannot reject a unit root; consider differencing
quiz.explain: ADF's null is a unit root (non-stationarity); a large p-value means no evidence against it.

concepts.name: ARIMA and SARIMAX forecasting
concepts.summary: Fit seasonal ARIMA models with exogenous regressors, check residuals and forecast with intervals.
concepts.why: ARIMA-family models are the standard statistical baseline for forecasting with honest uncertainty.
concepts.body:
An **ARIMA(p, d, q)** model differences the series d times, then predicts each value from its own previous p values (the **autoregressive** part) and from the previous q prediction errors (the moving-average part, unrelated to rolling means). **Seasonal** ARIMA adds `(P, D, Q, s)` terms at the seasonal lag s (12 for monthly data). **SARIMAX** further adds outside predictors known as **exogenous regressors**, such as price or holidays.

In statsmodels:

```python
from statsmodels.tsa.statespace.sarimax import SARIMAX
res = SARIMAX(y, exog=X, order=(1, 1, 1), seasonal_order=(0, 1, 1, 12)).fit(disp=False)
```

`statsmodels.tsa.arima.model.ARIMA` offers the same model with simpler arguments and more ways to estimate it.

Choosing orders: use ACF/PACF of the differenced series as a starting point, then compare candidates by AIC on the same data and by their error on a final period held out from fitting.

After fitting, check the residuals: `res.plot_diagnostics()` and `res.test_serial_correlation("ljungbox")` should show no remaining autocorrelation.

Forecasting: `fc = res.get_forecast(steps=12, exog=future_X)`, then `fc.predicted_mean` and `fc.conf_int()`. Exogenous regressors must be known (or forecast) for the future period. Intervals widen the further ahead you forecast (the horizon), as they should.

For a new observation, `res.append(new_y)` or `res.extend(new_y)` updates the model without refitting from scratch.
concepts.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from statsmodels.tsa.statespace.sarimax import SARIMAX

rng = np.random.default_rng(10)
idx = pd.date_range("2016-01-01", periods=96, freq="MS")
t = np.arange(96)
y = pd.Series(200 + 1.5 * t + 15 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * t / 12) + rng.normal(0, 3, 96), index=idx)
train, test = y[:-12], y[-12:]

res = SARIMAX(train, order=(1, 1, 1), seasonal_order=(0, 1, 1, 12)).fit(disp=False)
print(round(res.aic, 1))                              # 362.7

fc = res.get_forecast(steps=12)
mae = (fc.predicted_mean - test).abs().mean()
print(round(mae, 2))                                  # 2.75
print(fc.conf_int().iloc[[0, -1]].round(1).values.tolist())
# [[319.5, 329.8], [328.6, 339.2]]  (interval widens with horizon)
print(round(res.test_serial_correlation("ljungbox")[0, 1, -1], 2))  # 0.56 (no leftover autocorrelation)
takeaways: `order=(p, d, q)`, `seasonal_order=(P, D, Q, s)`, optional `exog`
Select by AIC and by error on a held-out final period
Check residual autocorrelation and use `get_forecast` for intervals
pitfalls: Evaluating a forecast model on randomly sampled points instead of a final hold-out period.

quiz.q: What must you provide to forecast a SARIMAX model that was fitted with exogenous regressors?
options: Future values of the exogenous regressors via exog=
quiz.explain: The model's predictions depend on the regressors, so their future values must be supplied.

concepts.name: Mixed effects models
concepts.summary: Model grouped or repeated-measures data with random intercepts and slopes using MixedLM.
concepts.why: Students in schools, patients measured over time and users across many visits are not independent rows.
concepts.body:
When data are grouped, observations within a group share something unobserved. A **linear mixed model** represents that with **random effects**: each group's own shift up or down, treated as drawn from a normal distribution, estimated alongside the usual coefficients, here called **fixed effects**.

`smf.mixedlm("score ~ hours", data=df, groups=df["school"]).fit()` gives each school its own random intercept. Add random slopes with `re_formula="~hours"`, letting the effect of hours vary by school too.

Reading the results:

- fixed effects (`res.fe_params`) are population-level effects, interpreted like OLS coefficients,
- `Group Var` in the summary is the variance of the random intercepts; compare it with the residual variance (`res.scale`) to see how much variation is between groups (the share of the total is the **intraclass correlation**),
- `res.random_effects` gives each group's estimated deviation, shrunk towards zero for small groups (**partial pooling**).

Why not dummies per group? Mixed models generalise to new groups, handle many small groups gracefully, and let you include group-level predictors that would be collinear with group dummies.

Fitting uses REML (restricted maximum likelihood, which gives less biased variance estimates) by default; set `reml=False` when comparing models with different fixed effects by likelihood or AIC. Convergence warnings are common with complex random effects; simplify the random structure or rescale predictors. For non-normal outcomes, `BinomialBayesMixedGLM` exists, and GEE is an alternative when you only want effects averaged over the whole population.
concepts.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
school = np.repeat(np.arange(30), 20)                 # 30 schools x 20 students
hours = rng.uniform(0, 10, 600)
school_int = rng.normal(0, 4, 30)[school]             # schools differ in baseline
df = pd.DataFrame({"school": school, "hours": hours,
                   "score": 50 + 2 * hours + school_int + rng.normal(0, 3, 600)})

res = smf.mixedlm("score ~ hours", data=df, groups=df["school"]).fit()
print(res.fe_params.round(2).to_dict())        # {'Intercept': 50.6, 'hours': 1.99}
group_var = res.cov_re.iloc[0, 0]
print(round(group_var, 1), round(res.scale, 1))  # 29.5 9.7
print(round(group_var / (group_var + res.scale), 2))  # 0.75 (intraclass correlation)
print(round(res.random_effects[0].iloc[0], 2))   # 2.33 (school 0 above average)
takeaways: Random effects model group-level variation; fixed effects are population effects
Random intercepts via `groups=`, random slopes via `re_formula=`
Group estimates are shrunk towards the mean (partial pooling)
pitfalls: Ignoring grouping and treating repeated measurements as independent rows.

quiz.q: Why are estimated random effects for small groups pulled towards zero?
options: Partial pooling: little data means more reliance on the population distribution
quiz.explain: The model balances each group's data against the overall distribution, weighting it by how much data the group has.

concepts.name: ANOVA, multiple comparisons and power analysis
concepts.summary: Compare groups with ANOVA tables, adjust for multiple comparisons and size experiments with power analysis.
concepts.why: Designing an experiment with enough data, and testing many groups honestly, are core statistical skills.
concepts.body:
**ANOVA tables** (analysis of variance: how much each term contributes to explaining the outcome): `sm.stats.anova_lm(res, typ=2)` on a fitted OLS model gives an F-test per term. Type 2 tests each term after the others, and is a good default without interactions; with interactions and groups of unequal size, type 3 with `Sum` contrasts is common. `anova_lm(m1, m2)` compares nested models.

**Multiple comparisons**: after finding that groups differ, `pairwise_tukeyhsd(endog, groups)` from `statsmodels.stats.multicomp` tests all pairs while keeping the chance of even one false alarm across all of them (the **family-wise error rate**) at 5%. For an arbitrary list of p-values, `multipletests(pvals, method="fdr_bh")` from `statsmodels.stats.multitest` applies Holm, Bonferroni (both control the family-wise error rate) or Benjamini-Hochberg (`fdr_bh`, which controls the share of false alarms among the significant results, the **false discovery rate**), and others.

**Power analysis** answers "how many rows do I need?" before running an experiment. **Power** is the chance a study detects an effect of a given size if it's really there; 80% is the usual target. `statsmodels.stats.power` has classes such as `TTestIndPower`, `NormalIndPower` and `FTestAnovaPower`. Their `solve_power` method takes all but one of effect size, sample size, alpha (the p-value cut-off, usually 0.05) and power, and solves for the missing one. The **effect size** is the difference you want to detect, measured in standard deviations (Cohen's d for means), or from `proportion_effectsize(p1, p2)` for proportions.

Underpowered studies are a major source of unreliable findings: they miss real effects, and the significant results they do produce overstate the effect size. Fix the sample size in advance, and don't stop early the moment p dips below 0.05.
concepts.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from statsmodels.stats.multicomp import pairwise_tukeyhsd
from statsmodels.stats.power import NormalIndPower, TTestIndPower
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportion_effectsize

n = TTestIndPower().solve_power(effect_size=0.3, alpha=0.05, power=0.8)
print(round(n))                                  # 175 per group for d = 0.3

es = proportion_effectsize(0.12, 0.10)           # conversion 10% -> 12%
print(round(NormalIndPower().solve_power(es, alpha=0.05, power=0.8)))  # 3835 per group

rng = np.random.default_rng(12)
df = pd.DataFrame({"group": np.repeat(["A", "B", "C"], 30),
                   "y": np.r_[rng.normal(10, 2, 30), rng.normal(10.2, 2, 30), rng.normal(12, 2, 30)]})
tukey = pairwise_tukeyhsd(df["y"], df["group"])
print(tukey.reject.tolist())                     # [False, True, False] (A-B, A-C, B-C)
takeaways: `anova_lm(res, typ=2)` tests each term; Tukey HSD compares all pairs
`multipletests` adjusts lists of p-values (Holm, FDR)
Use `solve_power` to fix sample size before the experiment
pitfalls: Peeking at results repeatedly and stopping as soon as p < 0.05.

quiz.q: What happens to the required sample size per group if the effect size you want to detect halves?
quiz.explain: Required n scales with 1 / effect size squared, so halving the effect needs about four times the data.

concepts.name: State space models and the Kalman filter
concepts.summary: Use statsmodels' state space machinery: hidden-state models, smoothed estimates, missing data and custom models.
concepts.why: SARIMAX, ETS and unobserved components all run on one state space engine you can extend.
concepts.body:
Much of `statsmodels.tsa.statespace` is one general model: a hidden **state** (say, the true underlying level of sales) changes over time by a linear rule plus noise, and what you observe is a noisy linear function of it. The **Kalman filter** walks through the data in time order, updating its estimate of the state after each observation and computing the likelihood; the **smoother** then goes back over the data to give the best estimate of each state using all observations, past and future. SARIMAX, `UnobservedComponents`, `DynamicFactor`, `VARMAX` and `ExponentialSmoothing` in that module are all built on it.

Practical benefits:

- **Missing values** are handled natively: the filter simply skips the update step, and you still get smoothed estimates for the gaps.
- **Interpretable components**: `UnobservedComponents(y, level="local linear trend", freq_seasonal=[{"period": 12}])` estimates trend and seasonality as states; `res.smoothed_state` or `res.level.smoothed` give them.
- **Diagnostics and forecasts** with intervals come for free, and `res.simulate` draws scenarios.

To build a custom model, write a class that inherits from `sm.tsa.statespace.MLEModel`: declare `k_states`, fill system matrices (`design`, `transition`, `selection`, `state_cov`, `obs_cov`) in `__init__`, define `start_params` and `param_names`, and write `update(params)` to put parameters into the matrices. Optional `transform_params` keeps variances positive during optimisation. Then `fit()`, `smooth()` and `get_forecast()` work as for built-in models.

Large or long models can be slow; options such as `concentrate_scale=True` and good starting parameters help convergence.
concepts.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.api as sm

rng = np.random.default_rng(13)
idx = pd.date_range("2018-01-01", periods=72, freq="MS")
level = 100 + np.cumsum(rng.normal(0.5, 1.0, 72))            # slowly drifting level
y = pd.Series(level + 8 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * np.arange(72) / 12) + rng.normal(0, 1.5, 72), index=idx)
y.iloc[30:34] = np.nan                                      # a gap in the data

mod = sm.tsa.UnobservedComponents(y, level="local linear trend",
                                  freq_seasonal=[{"period": 12, "harmonics": 2}])
res = mod.fit(disp=False)

smoothed_level = res.level.smoothed
print(np.isnan(smoothed_level).sum())         # 0 (gap filled by the smoother)
print(round(np.abs(smoothed_level - level).mean(), 2))     # 0.77 (close to the true level)
print(res.get_forecast(6).predicted_mean.round(1).iloc[:2].tolist())  # [147.9, 151.4]
takeaways: SARIMAX, UnobservedComponents, VARMAX and more share one Kalman filter engine
Missing observations are handled natively by the filter and smoother
Subclass `MLEModel` to build custom state space models
pitfalls: Interpolating gaps before fitting a state space model, which understates uncertainty.

quiz.q: How does the Kalman filter treat a missing observation?
options: It skips the measurement update and only propagates the state
quiz.explain: With no observation the filter just predicts forward, and the smoother later refines the estimate using later data.

concepts.name: Custom maximum likelihood models
concepts.summary: Estimate any model you can write a log-likelihood for with GenericLikelihoodModel and get standard errors and tests for it.
concepts.why: When no built-in model matches how your data were generated, writing the likelihood gives you estimates and standard errors anyway.
concepts.body:
Maximum likelihood estimation picks parameters that make the observed data most probable. statsmodels' `GenericLikelihoodModel` (in `statsmodels.base.model`) turns a log-likelihood into a full model with the usual results object.

Write a class that inherits from it and implement `loglikeobs(params)`, returning the log-likelihood of **each observation** as an array (or `nloglikeobs`, its negative). Then:

- `fit(start_params=..., method="bfgs", maxiter=...)` optimises the total likelihood,
- standard errors come from the **Hessian** (the matrix of second derivatives of the log-likelihood, i.e. how sharply it curves around its peak) inverted; it is computed numerically unless you supply `score` (first derivatives) and `hessian`,
- `summary()`, `conf_int()`, `t_test()`, `wald_test()` and `cov_type="HC0"` (sandwich) standard errors all work.

Implementing per-observation log-likelihoods enables robust ("sandwich") standard errors, which use each observation's own first derivatives.

Practical points:

- Reparameterise constrained parameters: estimate `log(sigma)` instead of `sigma` so the optimiser can't step into invalid values; transform back and use the delta method (a standard formula for the standard error of a transformed estimate) for its standard error.
- Good starting values (for example OLS estimates) prevent many convergence failures.
- Use `scipy.stats` log-densities (`stats.norm.logpdf`, `stats.t.logpdf`) to write likelihoods accurately.
- Name parameters with `exog_names` or the `extra_params_names` argument so the summary is readable.

The same machinery underlies the built-in discrete and count models.
concepts.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
from statsmodels.base.model import GenericLikelihoodModel

class TRegression(GenericLikelihoodModel):
    """Linear regression with Student-t errors (robust to outliers)."""
    def loglikeobs(self, params):
        beta, log_scale, log_df = params[:-2], params[-2], params[-1]
        resid = self.endog - self.exog @ beta
        return stats.t.logpdf(resid, df=np.exp(log_df), scale=np.exp(log_scale))

rng = np.random.default_rng(14)
x = rng.uniform(0, 10, 300)
y = 1 + 2 * x + stats.t.rvs(df=3, size=300, random_state=rng)
X = np.column_stack([np.ones(300), x])

mod = TRegression(y, X, extra_params_names=["log_scale", "log_df"])
res = mod.fit(start_params=[0, 1, 0, 1], method="bfgs", disp=0)
print(res.params.round(2))            # [0.91 1.99 0.   1.15]
print(res.bse[:2].round(3))           # [0.139 0.024]
print(round(np.exp(res.params[-1]), 1))  # 3.2 (estimated degrees of freedom)
takeaways: Implement `loglikeobs` returning per-observation log-likelihoods
Reparameterise constrained parameters (log scale) and give good start values
You get standard errors, tests and robust covariances for free
pitfalls: Returning the total log-likelihood from loglikeobs instead of one value per observation.

quiz.q: Why estimate log(sigma) instead of sigma in a custom likelihood?
options: The optimiser can then never propose a negative scale
It removes the need for start values
quiz.explain: Any real number maps to a positive sigma, so unconstrained optimisers stay in the valid region.

concepts.name: Convergence, separation and identification
concepts.summary: Diagnose failed or misleading fits: non-convergence, perfect separation, collinearity and unidentified parameters.
concepts.why: Fits that silently fail produce enormous or meaningless estimates that look like results.
concepts.body:
Models without a direct formula for their coefficients (Logit, GLM, MixedLM, ARIMA, custom likelihoods) are fitted by an **optimiser**: an algorithm that improves its guess step by step until it stops changing (it **converges**). They can fail in ways a summary doesn't make obvious. Learn the symptoms.

**Non-convergence**: a `ConvergenceWarning`, `res.mle_retvals["converged"] == False`, or a summary note. Remedies: rescale predictors to similar magnitudes, give better `start_params`, raise `maxiter`, or switch optimiser (`method="newton"`, `"bfgs"`, `"lbfgs"`, `"nm"`). Comparing estimates across two methods is a cheap sanity check.

**Perfect separation** in binary models: a predictor (or combination) predicts the outcome exactly, so the likelihood keeps increasing as the coefficient grows to infinity. Symptoms: `PerfectSeparationWarning`, huge coefficients with huge standard errors. Fixes: penalised estimation, which adds a cost for large coefficients and so keeps them finite, with `fit_regularized(alpha=..., L1_wt=0)` (ridge-style penalty); merging rare categories; or reconsidering the variable.

**Collinearity and identification**: if columns are linearly dependent (all dummies plus an intercept, or `total = a + b` together with a and b), the coefficients are not **identified**: infinitely many combinations fit equally well. OLS still returns one of them, but individual coefficients are arbitrary. Recent versions emit a `SingularMatrixWarning`, and the summary warns of a small eigenvalue. Check that `np.linalg.matrix_rank(res.model.exog)`, the number of truly independent columns in the design matrix, equals the number of columns.

**Boundary estimates**: variance components estimated at zero in mixed models, or ARIMA estimates right at the edge of what is allowed (non-stationary or nearly cancelling terms), signal a model with more parts than the data support.

Treat warnings as errors during development (`warnings.simplefilter("error")`) so these never slip into reports.
concepts.code:
import warnings
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

df = pd.DataFrame({"x": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8], "y": [0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1]})  # x > 4.5 -> y = 1

with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as w:
    warnings.simplefilter("always")
    res = smf.logit("y ~ x", data=df).fit(disp=0, maxiter=100)
print(sorted({type(x.message).__name__ for x in w}))
# ['ConvergenceWarning', 'PerfectSeparationWarning']
print(abs(res.params["x"]) > 10)          # True (coefficient running off to infinity)

reg = smf.logit("y ~ x", data=df).fit_regularized(alpha=1.0, L1_wt=0.0, disp=0)
print(reg.params.round(2).to_dict())      # {'Intercept': -0.65, 'x': 0.27} (finite, shrunk)

df["x2"] = 2 * df["x"]                     # perfectly collinear copy
exog = smf.ols("y ~ x + x2", data=df).fit().model.exog
print(np.linalg.matrix_rank(exog), exog.shape[1])   # 2 3 + SingularMatrixWarning
takeaways: Treat convergence and separation warnings as failures, not noise
Rescale, give start values or switch optimiser when fits don't converge
Check the design matrix rank; collinear columns make coefficients arbitrary
pitfalls: Reporting coefficients from a fit that emitted a ConvergenceWarning.

quiz.q: A logit fit returns a coefficient of 45 with a standard error of 9000. What is the likely cause?
options: A very strong but well-estimated effect
quiz.explain: Under separation the likelihood has no finite maximum, so the estimate and its uncertainty explode.
